hook.text: A sponge diver off Turkey found the richest ancient shipwreck ever — a 3,300-year-old floating department store.

buildup.text: The Uluburun wreck carried copper, tin, gold, ivory, amber, ebony, and glass from at least seven different cultures.

discovery.text: One ton of tin and ten tons of copper were on board — enough to make 300 bronze weapons.

twist.text: A golden scarab bearing Queen Nefertiti's name was among the cargo.

climax.text: The wreck proved that Bronze Age trade networks were far more connected and sophisticated than anyone had imagined.

punchline.text: One sunken ship rewrote the Bronze Age. The sea kept the evidence for 3,300.

quiz.question: What did the Uluburun shipwreck reveal about the Bronze Age?
options: Maritime trade did not exist before the Iron Age
Trade networks were far more connected and sophisticated than previously imagined
Only the Egyptians were capable of long-distance sea voyages

hook.text: Greek sponge divers found a Roman shipwreck in 1900 that contained the world's first known analog computer.

buildup.text: The ship sank around 60 BCE near Antikythera island, carrying bronze statues, jewelry, glassware, and coins.

discovery.text: Among the corroded lumps was a gear mechanism with over 30 bronze wheels — it predicted eclipses and planetary.

twist.text: Nothing this complex appeared again for 1,400 years. The technology was lost when Rome fell and was not reinvented.

climax.text: X-ray imaging in 2006 revealed inscriptions and gear teeth. The full device is now digitally reconstructed.

punchline.text: Ancient Greeks built a computer. The sea hid it for 2,000 years.

quiz.question: What was the Antikythera Mechanism used for?
options: Navigating ships across the open Mediterranean
Predicting eclipses and tracking planetary positions
Calculating taxes owed to the Roman Senate

hook.text: Greek triremes won the Battle of Salamis in 480 BCE. For centuries, no one could find a single wreck.

buildup.text: Triremes had three rows of oars and 170 rowers. They were fast, maneuverable, and built to ram enemy ships.

discovery.text: In 2016, divers found 22 wrecks near the Fourni archipelago in Greece — several with trireme-era construction.

twist.text: Triremes were built from thin planks and designed for speed, not durability. Most rotted away within years of sinking.

climax.text: A full-size replica called Olympias was built in 1987. Volunteer rowers proved it could reach nine knots — remarkably.

punchline.text: The ships that saved Greece were built to be fast, not to last.

quiz.question: Why are ancient trireme wrecks so rare?
options: The Greek navy recycled all damaged ships
They were built from thin planks that rotted quickly after sinking
Triremes were too small to be detected by modern sonar

hook.text: A perfectly preserved Viking ship was found buried in clay at the bottom of a Norwegian fjord — sails and all.

buildup.text: The Oseberg ship from 834 CE was a burial vessel for two wealthy women, filled with carts, textiles.

discovery.text: Five sunken Viking warships were found blocking a harbor at Skuldelev, Denmark — deliberately sunk to stop an invasion.

twist.text: One Skuldelev ship was 98 feet long and carried 60 warriors. It was built in Dublin — a Viking-Irish hybrid vessel.

climax.text: The wrecks proved Vikings had at least five different ship types: warships, traders, ferries, fishing boats.

punchline.text: Vikings built an entire navy with specialized designs.

quiz.question: What was discovered about the Skuldelev Viking ships?
options: They were all identical warships from the same fleet
They had at least five different types: warships, traders, ferries, fishing boats, and cargo
They were ceremonial vessels that never sailed on open water

topics.title: The Kyrenia Ship: Ancient Greek Merchant

hook.text: A Greek merchant ship from 300 BCE was found off Cyprus with its cargo of almonds and wine still intact.

buildup.text: The Kyrenia ship was a small coastal trader — 47 feet long, carrying 400 amphorae of wine and 10,000 almonds.

discovery.text: Lead sheathing on the hull protected against shipworms. The Greeks invented anti-fouling technology 2,300 years ago.

twist.text: The ship shows signs of pirate attack: spearheads embedded in the hull and cargo scattered as if searched.

climax.text: A full-size sailing replica was built and crossed the Mediterranean, proving the original design was fully seaworthy.

punchline.text: Pirates sank a wine ship. The sea aged it for 2,300 years.

quiz.question: What evidence of violence was found on the Kyrenia ship?
options: Burned timber from a fire attack
Spearheads embedded in the hull and scattered cargo suggesting a pirate attack
Sword marks on the mast from a boarding party

topics.title: The Mahdia Wreck: Rome's Art Collection

hook.text: A ship carrying looted Greek art to Rome sank off Tunisia around 80 BCE. Divers found the cargo in 1907.

buildup.text: The Mahdia wreck held bronze and marble statues, ornate furniture, and architectural columns from Athens.

discovery.text: The bronze statues were museum quality. Roman generals plundered Greek cities and shipped the art home as war trophies.

twist.text: Seawater preserved the bronzes better than air would have. Most ancient bronzes on land were melted for reuse.

climax.text: Underwater wrecks may hold more surviving ancient bronze statues than all the world's museums combined.

punchline.text: The art Rome stole from Greece survived because the ship sank before it arrived.

quiz.question: Why do shipwrecks often preserve bronze statues better than land sites?
options: Salt water creates a protective chemical coating on bronze
Bronzes on land were usually melted down for reuse over the centuries
Bronze reacts with sand to form a harder, more durable alloy

hook.text: In 1588, Spain sent 130 ships to invade England. Storms wrecked dozens along the coasts of Ireland and Scotland.

buildup.text: The English fleet used fire ships and long-range cannons to scatter the Armada into the North Sea.

discovery.text: Divers have found cannons, anchors, gold coins, and personal items from Armada wrecks off the Irish coast.

twist.text: Many sailors who survived the wrecks were killed by locals on shore.

climax.text: The Girona wreck off Northern Ireland yielded a gold salamander pendant and a ruby ring — personal treasures of Spanish.

punchline.text: Spain sent 130 ships. The sea returned jewelry, cannons.

quiz.question: What happened to many Spanish Armada sailors who survived the wrecks?
options: They were welcomed and settled permanently in Ireland
They were killed by locals since Ireland was English territory
They were captured and ransomed back to Spain

hook.text: The Nuestra Señora de Atocha sank in a hurricane in 1622 carrying 40 tons of gold and silver. It took 16 years to find.

buildup.text: Mel Fisher spent 16 years and his life savings searching for the Atocha off the Florida Keys.

discovery.text: In 1985, his team found the mother lode: gold bars, silver coins, emeralds, and gold chains worth over $450 million.

twist.text: The state of Florida sued Fisher for the treasure. The case went to the Supreme Court, which ruled the treasure was his.

climax.text: Critics argued that treasure hunters destroy archaeological context. Fisher's team kept no proper excavation records.

punchline.text: He found $450 million in gold. He lost the history it could have told.

quiz.question: Why did archaeologists criticize Mel Fisher's Atocha recovery?
options: He sold the treasure to private collectors instead of museums
His team kept no proper excavation records, destroying archaeological context
He used explosives that damaged the wreck site

topics.title: The Vasa: A Warship That Never Fought

hook.text: Sweden's mightiest warship sank on its maiden voyage in 1628 — in full view of thousands of spectators.

buildup.text: The Vasa was top-heavy with 64 cannons and ornate carvings. A gust of wind tipped it over just 1,300 yards from shore.

discovery.text: It was raised in 1961, 98 percent intact. Cold, brackish water preserved the wood for 333 years.

twist.text: The king had demanded more cannons than the design could support. Engineers knew it was unstable but feared telling him.

climax.text: The Vasa is now in its own museum in Stockholm — the world's best-preserved 17th-century ship.

punchline.text: A king's ego sank a warship. The sea preserved the embarrassment for 333 years.

quiz.question: Why did the Vasa sink on its maiden voyage?
options: It struck an uncharted rock near the harbor entrance
It was top-heavy with too many cannons and capsized in a gust of wind
A fire in the gunpowder magazine caused an explosion

topics.title: The Mary Rose: Henry VIII's Flagship

hook.text: Henry VIII watched helplessly from shore as his favorite warship sank during a French attack in 1545.

buildup.text: The Mary Rose capsized in the Solent, drowning most of its 400-man crew. Open gun ports let water flood in as it turned.

discovery.text: Raised in 1982, the wreck contained 19,000 artifacts: longbows, medical kits, backgammon sets.

twist.text: Facial reconstruction and DNA analysis of the crew revealed men from Africa and Southern Europe — Tudor England was.

climax.text: The Mary Rose is now displayed in Portsmouth with its artifacts — a complete snapshot of Tudor life at sea.

punchline.text: A king's warship sank with a pet dog, board games, and a multinational crew.

quiz.question: What did DNA analysis of the Mary Rose crew reveal?
options: All crew members were from the same English county
The crew included men from Africa and Southern Europe — Tudor England was diverse
Most sailors were former prisoners pressed into naval service

topics.title: The San José: The Holy Grail of Shipwrecks

hook.text: A Spanish galleon carrying $17 billion in gold sank off Colombia in 1708. Three countries are fighting over it.

buildup.text: The San José was sunk by British warships during the War of Spanish Succession. Its treasure was never recovered.

discovery.text: Colombia announced the wreck's discovery in 2015. Cameras showed cannons, ceramics, and gold coins on the seabed.

twist.text: Spain says the ship is theirs. Colombia says it is in their waters. A U.S.

climax.text: The legal battle highlights a global problem: who owns wrecks — the flag state, the coastal nation, or the finder?

punchline.text: Seventeen billion dollars on the seabed. Three countries, zero agreement.

quiz.question: Why is the San José shipwreck legally controversial?
options: It contains human remains that families want left undisturbed
Spain, Colombia, and a U.S. company all claim ownership
UNESCO has declared it off-limits to all salvage operations

hook.text: China once had the world's largest navy — ships five times bigger than Columbus's — and then destroyed it.

buildup.text: Admiral Zheng He led seven voyages from 1405 to 1433, reaching Africa with fleets of over 300 ships.

discovery.text: Wreck fragments found in Kenya and Sri Lanka match Chinese ceramics and coins from Zheng He's era.

twist.text: After Zheng He died, the emperor banned ocean voyages and burned the fleet's records. China turned inward for centuries.

climax.text: If the treasure fleet survived, China might have colonized Africa before Europe did.

punchline.text: China had the world's biggest fleet and chose to burn it. Europe sailed instead.

quiz.question: What happened to China's treasure fleet after Zheng He's voyages?
options: It was defeated by a coalition of Southeast Asian navies
The emperor banned ocean voyages and the fleet's records were burned
It continued trading under private merchants for another century

hook.text: Cleopatra's royal palace lies underwater in the harbor of Alexandria.

buildup.text: Franck Goddio began mapping the site in 1996 and found columns, sphinxes, and statues scattered across the harbor floor.

discovery.text: A colossal granite statue of a Ptolemaic pharaoh was raised from the mud, standing over 16 feet tall.

twist.text: The famous Lighthouse of Alexandria — one of the Seven Wonders — also collapsed into the harbor.

climax.text: Egypt plans an underwater museum where visitors can view the ruins through glass tunnels beneath the harbor.

punchline.text: Cleopatra's palace is 20 feet underwater. Egypt plans to let visitors walk.

quiz.question: What caused Alexandria's royal quarter to sink?
options: Rising sea levels gradually flooded the coastline
Earthquakes dropped the structures into the harbor about 1,600 years ago
A tsunami from a volcanic eruption destroyed the foundations

hook.text: Hindu scripture says the god Krishna's golden city sank beneath the waves.

buildup.text: The Mahabharata places Dwarka on India's western coast in Gujarat.

discovery.text: Marine archaeologists found stone walls, anchors, and pottery off the Gujarat coast dating to around 1500 BCE.

twist.text: The ruins cannot prove the mythological story, but they do prove a significant ancient port existed at the legendary.

climax.text: Millions of pilgrims visit the Dwarka temple each year, convinced the underwater city is Krishna's real kingdom.

punchline.text: Myth described a sunken city. The sea floor had one waiting to be found.

quiz.question: What is the archaeological challenge with Dwarka?
options: The site is too deep for divers to properly investigate
The ruins confirm an ancient port but cannot prove the mythological story
Modern construction has completely destroyed the underwater evidence

hook.text: Rome's most exclusive resort town is now underwater. You can snorkel over marble floors and villa walls.

buildup.text: Baiae was where Rome's elite went to party. Emperors, senators, and the wealthy built seaside villas with heated pools.

discovery.text: Volcanic activity in the Campi Flegrei area slowly lowered the coastline, sinking the town beneath the Bay of Naples.

twist.text: The ruins are so well preserved that mosaics, statues, and garden paths remain clearly visible beneath the waves.

climax.text: Baiae is now a marine protected area. Glass-bottom boat tours let visitors see Roman luxury beneath the waves.

punchline.text: Rome's playground for the rich is now a snorkeling site for tourists.

quiz.question: What caused the Roman resort town of Baiae to sink?
options: An earthquake collapsed the cliffs it was built on
Volcanic activity slowly lowered the coastline below sea level
Rising sea levels after the Roman Warm Period flooded the shore

hook.text: The Lighthouse of Alexandria was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

buildup.text: Built around 280 BCE, the Pharos stood over 300 feet tall and guided ships into Alexandria for over 1,000 years.

discovery.text: Earthquakes between 956 and 1323 CE gradually toppled it. Divers found massive stone blocks on the harbor floor in 1994.

twist.text: Qaitbay Fortress, built on the lighthouse site in 1480, used some of the fallen lighthouse stones in its own walls.

climax.text: Underwater surveys mapped over 2,500 blocks from the lighthouse.

punchline.text: A Wonder of the World fell into the sea. Its stones built a medieval fort.

quiz.question: What happened to the Pharos Lighthouse of Alexandria?
options: It was deliberately demolished by conquering armies
Earthquakes gradually toppled it into the harbor between 956 and 1323 CE
It was dismantled and shipped to Rome by Emperor Augustus

topics.title: Pavlopetri: Walking on a Sunken Town

hook.text: The oldest known submerged city sits in just 12 feet of water off southern Greece. You can swim right over it.

buildup.text: Pavlopetri dates to 2800 BCE and has streets, houses, tombs, and a possible town square — all on the seabed.

discovery.text: Nicholas Flemming discovered it in 1967 while snorkeling. He spotted walls and realized they were man-made.

twist.text: Earthquakes around 1000 BCE submerged it. The seabed preserved walls that erosion on land would have destroyed long ago.

climax.text: 3D digital mapping in 2009 revealed a complete Bronze Age town plan — the most detailed ever found underwater.

punchline.text: A 5,000-year-old town sits in snorkeling depth. History is twelve feet down.

quiz.question: What makes Pavlopetri archaeologically unique?
options: It is the deepest submerged city ever discovered
It is the oldest known submerged city in the world
It contains the only underwater temple ever found

topics.title: Port Royal: The Sunken Pirate Capital

hook.text: Jamaica's pirate capital sank in 1692 when an earthquake liquefied the sand beneath it. Two-thirds vanished in minutes.

buildup.text: Port Royal was the richest and most notorious city in the Caribbean — a haven for buccaneers and rum traders.

discovery.text: Underwater excavations found a stopped watch, tavern signs, pewter plates, and a chest of pirate coins.

twist.text: The liquefaction swallowed buildings whole. Some structures sank vertically with furniture still inside the rooms.

climax.text: Port Royal is one of the best-preserved underwater urban sites. The mud sealed everything like a time capsule.

punchline.text: Earthquakes turned sand to liquid and swallowed a pirate city whole.

quiz.question: How were Port Royal's buildings so well preserved underwater?
options: Coral grew over the structures and protected them
Buildings sank vertically in liquefied sand, and mud sealed them like a time capsule
Cold Caribbean currents prevented decay of organic materials

hook.text: The 'unsinkable' Titanic hit an iceberg on April 15, 1912, and sank in under three hours, killing 1,517 people.

buildup.text: The wreck lay undiscovered at 12,500 feet for 73 years. Robert Ballard found it in 1985 using deep-sea cameras.

discovery.text: The ship broke in two on the way down. The bow section is embedded 60 feet into the mud. The stern is shattered.

twist.text: Iron-eating bacteria are consuming the hull. Scientists estimate the wreck will be completely gone by 2030.

climax.text: In 2023, a submersible visiting the wreck imploded, killing five passengers. The Titanic still claims lives.

punchline.text: The Titanic is disappearing. Bacteria are finishing what the iceberg started.

quiz.question: What is happening to the Titanic wreck?
options: Treasure hunters are dismantling it piece by piece
Iron-eating bacteria are consuming the hull and may destroy it by 2030
Deep ocean currents are burying it deeper into the seabed

hook.text: Germany's mightiest battleship was sunk in 1941 after a chase across the Atlantic. It sat undiscovered for 48 years.

buildup.text: The Bismarck sank HMS Hood in minutes, then the entire Royal Navy hunted it down. Torpedoes crippled its rudder.

discovery.text: Robert Ballard found it in 1989 sitting upright on a volcanic mountain 15,000 feet deep — remarkably intact.

twist.text: Damage analysis suggests the crew scuttled the ship themselves to prevent British capture. They sank their own pride.

climax.text: The wreck is a war grave. Over 2,000 German sailors died. International law protects it from salvage.

punchline.text: The crew sank their own ship. The sea guards it as a tomb.

quiz.question: What does damage analysis suggest happened to the Bismarck?
options: British bombs caused the fatal explosion
The German crew scuttled the ship themselves to prevent capture
A torpedo hit the ammunition magazine, causing it to explode

topics.title: The USS Indianapolis: A Tragic Discovery

hook.text: A U.S. cruiser was torpedoed in 1945 after delivering parts for the atomic bomb. 900 men went into the water.

buildup.text: The Navy did not notice the ship was missing for four days. Sailors drifted in shark-infested waters without lifeboats.

discovery.text: Only 316 of the 1,195 crew survived. It remains the worst single-ship loss in U.S. Navy history.

twist.text: The captain was court-martialed for the sinking. His record was not cleared until 2001, decades after his suicide.

climax.text: Paul Allen's research vessel found the wreck in 2017 at 18,000 feet — the ship was remarkably well preserved.

punchline.text: They delivered the bomb that ended a war. Nobody came to save them.

quiz.question: Why was the loss of the USS Indianapolis so devastating?
options: The ship was carrying thousands of civilian refugees
The Navy didn't notice it was missing for four days while survivors drifted
It was the largest warship ever sunk by a submarine

hook.text: Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance was crushed by Antarctic ice in 1915. It was found in 2022, perfectly preserved.

buildup.text: The ship sank in the Weddell Sea after being trapped in pack ice for months. Shackleton led all 27 men to safety.

discovery.text: A search team found it 10,000 feet deep using autonomous underwater vehicles.

twist.text: Cold Antarctic water and lack of wood-eating organisms preserved the ship almost perfectly — the masts still stand.

climax.text: The wreck is protected as a historic monument under the Antarctic Treaty. No artifacts may be removed.

punchline.text: The ice crushed it. The cold saved it. Endurance lived up to its name.

quiz.question: Why was the Endurance so well preserved after 107 years?
options: A thick layer of sediment quickly buried and sealed the wreck
Cold Antarctic water and the absence of wood-eating organisms preserved it
The ship's oak construction was naturally resistant to decay

hook.text: The USS Arizona has been leaking oil since it sank on December 7, 1941. Visitors call the drops 'black tears.'

buildup.text: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor sank or damaged 21 ships and killed 2,403 Americans in under two hours.

discovery.text: The Arizona was never raised. A memorial was built directly above the sunken hull, which is visible through the water.

twist.text: The ship still holds an estimated 500,000 gallons of fuel oil.

climax.text: Corrosion is weakening the hull. The Navy monitors it constantly, balancing preservation with ecological risk.

punchline.text: The Arizona still bleeds oil 80 years later. The war is not over for the ship.

quiz.question: What ongoing risk does the USS Arizona wreck pose?
options: Unexploded ammunition could detonate at any time
Corrosion could cause a collapse releasing 500,000 gallons of fuel oil
The memorial structure above is sinking into the wreck

hook.text: A modern passenger ferry sank in the Baltic Sea in 1994, killing 852 people.

buildup.text: The MS Estonia was sailing from Tallinn to Stockholm in heavy seas when its bow visor broke off, flooding the car deck.

discovery.text: The ship sank in 35 minutes. Most passengers were asleep. Only 137 survived the freezing Baltic waters.

twist.text: Sweden and Estonia sealed the wreck site and made it illegal to dive there. Families accused governments of a cover-up.

climax.text: A 2020 documentary found a large hole in the hull not in original reports. New investigations were launched.

punchline.text: A sealed wreck and a hidden hole. The truth may still be at the bottom of.

quiz.question: Why did the MS Estonia disaster become controversial?
options: The ferry company denied the ship had any safety issues
Governments sealed the wreck and a documentary found damage not in original reports
Insurance companies refused to pay claims to the victims' families

topics.title: SCUBA and the Birth of Underwater Archaeology

hook.text: Before SCUBA, underwater archaeology did not exist. Jacques Cousteau's invention in 1943 created an entire field.

buildup.text: Cousteau and Émile Gagnan developed the Aqua-Lung, which let divers breathe freely and work underwater for the first.

discovery.text: Cousteau led one of the first underwater excavations at Grand Congloué in 1952, recovering Roman amphorae from a wreck.

twist.text: Early divers used airlifts that sucked up artifacts and sediment — destroying context.

climax.text: George Bass pioneered scientific underwater excavation in the 1960s.

punchline.text: Cousteau let us breathe underwater. Bass taught us to think underwater.

quiz.question: Who is considered the pioneer of scientific underwater excavation?
options: Jacques Cousteau, who invented the Aqua-Lung
George Bass, who applied land archaeology methods to underwater sites
Robert Ballard, who discovered the Titanic

topics.title: ROVs and AUVs: Robots in the Deep

hook.text: Robots now explore shipwrecks at depths where humans cannot survive — mapping sites no diver will ever reach.

buildup.text: ROVs (Remotely Operated Vehicles) are tethered robots with cameras and manipulator arms controlled from the surface.

discovery.text: AUVs (Autonomous Underwater Vehicles) swim independently, scanning vast areas of seabed with sonar and cameras.

twist.text: An AUV found the Endurance at 10,000 feet. It operated under Antarctic ice where no human could have searched.

climax.text: Deep-sea robots are discovering wrecks faster than archaeologists can study them. The technology outpaces the workforce.

punchline.text: Robots can now find wrecks anywhere. The hard part is having enough humans to.

quiz.question: What is the difference between ROVs and AUVs?
options: ROVs work only in freshwater while AUVs work in saltwater
ROVs are tethered and controlled from the surface; AUVs swim independently
ROVs are used for photography while AUVs are used for excavation

hook.text: Sonar can reveal a shipwreck hidden under sand and mud without anyone getting wet. Sound sees what eyes cannot.

buildup.text: Side-scan sonar tows a sensor behind a ship, sending sound waves sideways across the seabed and recording the echoes.

discovery.text: The resulting images show objects on the bottom in remarkable detail — cannons, anchors.

twist.text: Most 'wrecks' detected by sonar turn out to be rocks or modern debris. False positives waste months of dive time.

climax.text: Multibeam sonar now creates 3D seabed maps accurate to inches. Entire coastlines can be surveyed in days.

punchline.text: We can now map the ocean floor like a city street. Most of it is still unmapped.

quiz.question: What is a major challenge with side-scan sonar wreck detection?
options: Sound waves cannot penetrate deeper than 100 feet
Most detected objects turn out to be rocks or debris, not wrecks
Sonar only works in warm tropical waters

hook.text: Thousands of overlapping photos can build a perfect 3D model of a shipwreck — freezing an entire site in digital time.

buildup.text: Divers or robots photograph every angle of a wreck. Software stitches the images into a centimeter-accurate 3D model.

discovery.text: Archaeologists can study a site remotely, zoom in on details, and share models with colleagues worldwide.

twist.text: The technique works on sites too deep or dangerous to revisit. Once scanned, the model outlasts the wreck itself.

climax.text: Public museums now display interactive 3D wreck models. Anyone with a browser can explore a Roman shipwreck from home.

punchline.text: You can now explore a 2,000-year-old shipwreck from your couch.

quiz.question: Why is 3D photogrammetry valuable for underwater archaeology?
options: It replaces the need for divers entirely
Digital models outlast the wreck and can be studied remotely by anyone
It can reveal artifacts hidden inside sealed containers

topics.title: Conservation: Saving What the Sea Gives Back

hook.text: Pulling an artifact from the sea is easy. Keeping it from crumbling to dust afterward is the hard part.

buildup.text: Waterlogged wood shrinks and cracks when it dries. Metal corrodes rapidly once exposed to air after centuries.

discovery.text: The Vasa warship spent 17 years being sprayed with polyethylene glycol to replace water in its wood cells.

twist.text: Some objects are better left on the seabed. Raising them without proper facilities can destroy them faster than the sea.

climax.text: Conservation costs often exceed excavation costs. Many underwater finds wait years in water tanks for treatment.

punchline.text: Finding a wreck takes skill. Keeping it intact after takes patience, chemistry.

quiz.question: Why can raising artifacts from the sea actually damage them?
options: Sunlight bleaches all underwater pigments immediately
Waterlogged wood shrinks and metal corrodes rapidly once exposed to air
The change in water pressure causes artifacts to expand and crack

topics.title: The UNESCO Convention on Underwater Heritage

hook.text: For centuries, underwater finds belonged to whoever pulled them up first. Then the rules changed.

buildup.text: Treasure hunters destroyed thousands of wrecks for profit, ripping out valuable objects and discarding the rest.

discovery.text: UNESCO's 2001 Convention on Underwater Cultural Heritage set rules: no commercial exploitation of wrecks over 100 years.

twist.text: Major maritime nations like the U.S. and UK have not signed it. Enforcement remains weak in international waters.

climax.text: An estimated three million shipwrecks lie on the world's ocean floors. Most are unprotected and at risk.

punchline.text: Three million wrecks. One treaty. Most of the world has not signed it.

quiz.question: What does the 2001 UNESCO Convention on Underwater Cultural Heritage do?
options: It gives all shipwrecks to the country whose flag the ship flew
It bans commercial exploitation of wrecks over 100 years old
It requires all underwater finds to be placed in national museums
